n: Second Samuel picks up right where 1 Samuel ends. Saul has just died in battle, and David, back from rescuing his people’s families from Amalekite raiders, waits in Ziklag, the Philistine town where he had been living as an outlaw.

f.g: A town in the Negev given to David by Achish, the Philistine king of Gath (1 Samuel 27:6).

n: A messenger arrives showing every sign of mourning — torn clothes and dirt on his head. He bows low before David, as if already treating him as the new king.

f.g: Rent = torn. Tearing one’s garments and putting dust on the head were customary signs of grief or disaster.
Bowed down with his face to the ground as a sign of honor.

n: David asks where he has come from, and the man says he escaped from Israel’s army camp — a hint that the news is very bad.

f.g: Whence = from where.

n: The news is the worst possible: Israel has been routed, many are dead, and both King Saul and Jonathan, David’s dearest friend, have fallen.

f.w: Saul and Jonathan his son are dead

n: David does not simply accept the report. He presses the young man for proof, perhaps already sensing something is off in his story.
The Amalekite says he “happened by chance” on Mount Gilboa and found Saul leaning on his spear with enemy chariots closing in. His account differs from 1 Samuel 31, where Saul falls on his own sword.

f.g: A ridge at the eastern edge of the Jezreel Valley in northern Israel, where Saul made his last stand.

n: In his story, the wounded Saul spotted him and called out, and he answered as a willing servant.
He admits he is an Amalekite — a member of the very people Saul had been commanded to destroy, and whom David had just been fighting. The irony would not be lost on readers.
According to the man, Saul begged to be killed because he was in agony yet still alive.

f.g: The Hebrew word is rare; it may mean a cramp, dizziness, or the agony of a mortal wound.

n: He claims he finished Saul off and brought the king’s crown and armband to David. Most readers see him as an opportunist who stripped the body and invented the story, hoping for a reward from Saul’s rival.

f.g: Probably a royal headband or diadem rather than a large crown.

f.w: the bracelet that was on his arm
f.g: An armlet, a band worn on the upper arm as royal insignia.

n: Instead of celebrating, David and his men tear their clothes in grief. David had never wanted Saul’s death, even after years of being hunted by him.
They mourn and fast all day — not only for Saul and Jonathan, but for the whole nation and the army of the Lord that had been struck down.

f.g: Even = evening. Fasting until sunset was a common expression of mourning (compare 1 Samuel 31:13).

n: David asks again where the man is from. He calls himself the son of a “stranger” — a foreign resident living in Israel — which means he should have known Israel’s reverence for the anointed king.

f.g: Hebrew ger — a resident foreigner who lived among Israel and was expected to know its laws.

n: David is stunned: how could anyone dare to raise his hand against the man God had anointed? David himself had twice refused to kill Saul when he had the chance.
David orders the man executed. The bearer of “good news” finds that David will not reward anyone for violence against Saul’s house.

f.g: An idiom meaning to attack and kill him.

n: By his own words the Amalekite convicted himself. Whether his story was true or false, he claimed the deed, and David holds him responsible.

f.w: Thy blood be upon thy head
f.g: You are responsible for your own death; your guilt is your own.

f.w: thy mouth hath testified against thee

n: David now composes a lament — a poem of grief — for Saul and Jonathan. It is one of the most moving funeral songs in all of scripture.

f.g: A formal song of mourning sung over the dead.

n: The poem was taught to the people of Judah and preserved in an ancient collection called the book of Jasher, which is no longer extant. “The bow” may be the name of the song itself.

f.g: The words “the use of” are added by the translators; the Hebrew simply says “the Bow,” possibly the lament’s title, since Jonathan’s bow is honored in verse 22.
Jasher = “the upright one”; a lost book of Israelite poetry.

n: The lament opens with its refrain: Israel’s glory has been killed on the hills. “How are the mighty fallen” repeats three times, like a tolling bell.

f.g: Or “the glory” or “the gazelle” of Israel — a poetic title for Saul and Jonathan.
This refrain appears in verses 19, 25, and 27, framing the poem.

n: David does not want the Philistine cities to hear the news and gloat. Gath and Askelon were two of the five main Philistine cities.

f.g: A Philistine city, home of Goliath and of King Achish.
Ashkelon, a Philistine city on the Mediterranean coast.
A term for the Philistines, who did not share Israel’s covenant sign of circumcision.

n: In poetic grief David curses the mountains where Saul died: may no dew or rain fall there. Saul’s shield lies defiled, as if he had never been anointed king.

f.g: Fields whose harvest could provide offerings; David wishes the hills to be barren.
Warriors oiled leather shields to keep them supple; the phrase also echoes Saul’s anointing as king.

n: David honors the two men as warriors: Jonathan’s bow and Saul’s sword never came back from battle without striking the enemy.
David speaks generously of Saul, remembering the father and son as loved and united to the end. Jonathan had stayed loyal to his father even while loving David.

f.w: in their death they were not divided

n: He calls on Israel’s women to mourn Saul, who brought prosperity to the nation — the spoils of his victories became fine clothing and jewelry for them.

f.g: Fine red-dyed cloth, a costly luxury.

n: The refrain returns, now focusing on Jonathan, lying slain on the heights.

f.g: Here simply the hills or heights where the battle was fought.

n: David’s most personal words: Jonathan’s loyal, covenant love for him was extraordinary, deeper than any love he had known. Their friendship is one of scripture’s great examples of selfless devotion.

f.g: Passing = surpassing. David is describing a friendship of covenant loyalty that exceeded even marriage in faithfulness.

n: The poem ends with the refrain a final time. The “weapons of war” may be a poetic way of speaking of Saul and Jonathan themselves.

f.g: Likely a metaphor for the fallen warriors, Israel’s defenders.
